en: Inside the palace Aichürök—
The vast host of black Jediger
Could not force their way in
To the excited beauty.
The Jediger could not reach
And plunder your sister-in-law,
Though their vast army bent the earth;
They could neither loose bows nor fire guns.
The many Jediger could not brave
That accursed lioness of a woman.
The reason they could not enter:
Look at the moon risen over the mountain;
Look at the moon, then look at her face;
Look upon Chürök, whiter than the moon,
Upon her form of perfect grace.
There is the morning star in heaven—
Look at the star, then look at her eyes;
Look at sugar, then hear her words;
Look upon the gleaming form
Of that wretched fairy-born woman.
Her white breast exposed,
Her precious body gleaming,
The ill-fated woman of manly bearing
Worked out a plan in her mind:
She meant to leave the palace dead.
Thus the wretched woman’s purpose formed;
She clenched her teeth with all her strength.
“Let their heroes draw near;
Let me divide and judge
Their would-be lions,
Their fighters and their men;
Let me strike them with Zulpukor.
The skilled spearman,
Kanchoro who destroyed the village,
That mighty man and others like him;
Warrior Kyyaz, their khan,
That fatherless, ill-starred man—”
Taking courage, she clenched her teeth,
Counted her resources and formed her plan;
Your sister-in-law Aichürök prepared herself.
Their fighters and wrestlers,
Their men who boasted of strength,
Brandishing battle-axes and thrusting spears,
Closed around the wretched Chürök in the palace.
Their fighters and lions,
Their men who boasted of strength,
Swarmed all about her.
The Jediger pressed in
To bind her at last.
Their executioners and lions,
Each separate man,
Their many kinds of wrestlers,
Had only just surged forward
When valiant Aichürök
Caught hold of Zulpukor,
Which stood ready in its sheath,
And drew it by the hilt—
The blade that set grass afire when laid upon it,
And cut down at once whatever it struck,
The bloodthirsty hero’s Zulpukor.
She took the sword in hand.
Against the wrestlers surging in,
Against the men who meant to seize her,
The blustering, broad-chested men,
The men rushing in with battle-cries,
Matchless in her swiftness,
Aichürök of manly bearing
Took the sword in hand.
As the clamoring Jediger
Were about to turn and flee,
She took the sword in hand.
Before the wrestlers could scatter,
Before they could block the gate-mouth,
She drew the sword and stabbed,
Striking this way and that,
Whirling everything into dust,
Filling the gate-mouth with blood,
And laying their wrestlers low.
Aichürök fought with courage,
Refusing to yield to their force,
And your sister-in-law would not surrender
Her dear head to plunder.
They kept her tightly surrounded
And fought without pause many times.
The heedless Jediger rushed in;
The champions who had taken gold,
Who had plundered women and made them wail,
The heroes swollen with pride,
Were struck across the neck by her sword,
Blood pouring down their breasts.
Many men reeled in panic;
A tumult rose as they stampeded,
And many wrestlers fled.
Of the many wrestlers who met her,
Men lay dead.
The lions who boasted of strength
Were bodies without heads;
Some lay stretched on their backs,
And many wrestlers, many men,
Lay sprawled upon the ground.
Your sister-in-law had taken up the sword;
Of the fine champions who entered combat,
Each one a chosen steed among men,
All of them renowned heroes,
Aichürök slaughtered about a hundred
And cut off their heads.
They could not endure the heat
Of your grieving sister-in-law Chürök;
They could not approach her brow,
Could not seize her in the palace,
Could not make her their spoil,
Could not face and capture
The renowned khan’s fierce wife.
When they saw the ill-fated woman,
They lost their wits;
Having badly misjudged their plan,
They let the luckless woman
Cut down their warriors and khans.
Brave Kyyaz of the Jediger
Went to Khan Kanchoro:
“This woman Aichürök,
This quivering infidel,
This wayward-minded woman—
Her silk dress cannot be torn,
And she shows no sign of making peace.
She is a woman of another kind,
With a form unlike other women;
She skims along the white sash,
And has flown and traveled
Across the whole wide world.
Your unlucky sister-in-law
Clearly bears the mark of a champion;
She is hostile to men
And shows another nature.
Fair of face but treacherous within—
My friend Kanchoro,
This woman of yours is terribly dangerous.
When you take her to the Seven Rivers,
My friend, this raging wretch of yours
Will be the one to heap earth over you.
She is a consummate tyrant, a great predator,
A lone and cunning creature.
When you take this roaring infidel as wife,
May she not put poison in your food
And finish you off.
May she not pour poison into the bozo keg,
Poison that burns,
And blind you by gouging out your eyes.
May the age-old people not mock you,
Saying, ‘Kyyaz died by a woman
And saw in his breast
The true abode from which none return’;
May no fiddler in a house of daughters,
No servant attending a woman,
Make you the laughingstock of the age.
My friend, may the striking God not strike you!
May no champion who hears with ears and sees with eyes
Make mockery of you.
Let us not take this savage woman,
This roaring shrew.
When we take Aichürök
By fighting and dragging her away,
May she not bring us shameful disaster.
May she not neigh like a stallion
And keep us in torment;
May she not bring savage calamity.
Friend, heed me: Kyyaz must not take her.
As a wife she divided nations;
As a maiden, the notorious woman
Shook the age and divided peoples.
This is the celebrated Chürök;
No Chürök—this woman
Is a calamity that has ruined the world.
Those are the black eyes of the shrew;
No Chürök—your infidel
Is hell itself!
Let us not go down the path of ruin.
Let me turn back to my people;
My friend, I will not take this woman!”
Then Kanchoro
Readied himself like a hawk.
From Kanchoro’s mouth
Came wisdom as though from the unseen;
He shook himself from his agitation,
Stamped the earth in fury,
And spoke to brave Kyyaz:
“Your father’s grave, brave Kyyaz!
No brave Kyyaz, but earthbound Kyyaz!
Kyyaz, a span beneath a woman,
You are an infidel Kyyaz.
You regard even the lawful, white-paired wife
As something forbidden;
Your head bound up in wickedness,
You will not die leaving a single ewe.
If you continue like this, you will come to nothing.
The Seven Rivers, your land,
I had thought a true land.
Ah, brave Kyyaz fit to sink into the earth,
I had thought you a man.
You are no man, but mere earth;
You must be witless Kyyaz,
Strong only in your muddled fear,
Who imagines evil in a woman.
I had called you warrior Kyyaz—
Oh, my boy, you are womanly Kyyaz.
My friend, never until now
Have you twisted my words
And grieved me so, Kyyaz.
If you do not seize as spoil
The impetuous woman Chürök,
And return boasting
To your Seven Rivers, your land of Tarkan,
Saying, ‘I raised a tumult
Over Chürök, for whom Toltoy died;
I took the woman as spoil;
I avenged the old grievance,
The ancient rancor of brave Toltoy,’
If you cannot boast of that,
What sort of khan are you among the Kazakhs?
Where is the spirit in you
That sustains a people and keeps a nation?
You smashed her gate with axes,
And took her gold into your sacks;
You made the red-robed, slender-waisted
Maiden your spoil.
Yet when you met her face to face,
You grew terrified of Aichürök
And started a quarrel, wretched Kyyaz.
You took the renowned land of Talas,
Took the Argyn and Kyrgyz peoples,
Took Külchoro and giant Bakay,
And took countless thoroughbred herds.
The many champions who entered combat,
Every one of them renowned,
You took so many lions among men;
Yet now you shrink back,
Turning your neck as if to flee.
When truly challenged, she is your widow;
If you master yourself, she is your own wife,
Yet you stand afraid of a woman.
You babble, Kyyaz—
Whom do you think you are mocking?
You whimper, saying,
‘A woman slaughtered the wrestlers;
This is what a woman does when enraged,’
And you, warrior, turn soft.
If a woman frightens you so,
What will you do if bloodthirsty Semetey
Should suddenly return?
Can an enemy ever be spared?
If one of the tigers turns upon you,
Kyyaz, will begging save your life?
My friend, can these words be yours?
You have no spirit, Kyyaz;
You utter worthless talk
And take fright at a woman
